Ghost Rovers is a free web game for kids aged 10–14 about 25 machines NASA left on the Moon, Mars, Venus, in Earth orbit and deep space: what each did, where it is now and what is happening to it...

Kids read each machine's story as transmissions whose signal fades to "Last contact", then wake it with Mission Control decisions marked Real event or Training simulation. Rovers add a driving puzzle built around Mars signal delay. They message machines (simulated replies that wait the real light-speed time), point a phone at the sky to find them, hear stories read aloud, and take 5-question machine quizzes and 10-question Grand Quizzes. Each machine has a Tech Lab, facts and a Then & now card. There are live NASA Image Library photos, a live solar system map, 3D worlds, a Left Behind page and a Debrief vote on what to do with it all.

Waking machines, quizzes, replies and 16 badges earn Stardust and five ranks. The Moon is free; finishing a destination and spending Stardust unlocks Mars (150), Venus (300), Space Telescopes (450) and Deep Space (600). Progress saves on the device, or to the cloud with a free account...

Judges: no login needed. Click the "For judges" tab on the right edge for 2,000 Stardust, a guided 9-stop tour, and tester tools on the Badges & Stardust page (unlock all destinations, wake all machines, +1,000 Stardust, reset)...

Built with AI-assisted coding; designed by Team Earthlings.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Ghost Rovers is a free, browser-based story game for kids aged 10–14 about the hardware NASA has left behind on other worlds and in space. It features 25 real machines across five destinations: the Moon, Mars, Venus, Space Telescopes and Deep Space. The game asks one question: what did we leave behind, and what is happening to it now?

Each machine tells its own story in the first person, as a series of radio transmissions. For machines that have gone silent, the signal bars fade with every transmission until the last one reads "Last contact – No signal". Machines the player hasn't reached yet are shown "Asleep" in grey. To wake one up, the player completes a wake-up mission: a set of Mission Control decisions, each clearly labelled as a Real event (based on what actually happened) or a Training simulation (a practice situation built from real engineering). Rover missions add a driving puzzle: players plan up to 10 commands per Martian day, send them, and watch the rover move, just as real rover drivers do because of the signal delay. When a machine wakes, its photo comes back to life with "Signal acquired".

Every machine page also has a Tech Lab explaining its parts, "Did you know?" facts, a mission card, the science it made possible, and a Then & Now card showing where it is today, what space is doing to it and what it led to. A 5-question quiz checks understanding, and every answer can be found on that page. Each destination ends with a 10-question Grand Quiz with a 50:50 lifeline.

Kids can send messages to machines. The replies are simulated from each machine's real mission facts, but the waiting time is real: it is worked out from the machine's actual distance today and the speed of light (about 24 hours each way for Voyager 1). On a phone, the sky finder uses location and compass to point kids at the Moon, Mars, Venus, Webb's direction or deep-space probes like Voyager 1 and New Horizons, turning green when they are on target. A Listen button reads stories and replies aloud.

Other parts of the site: a live solar-system map with real planet positions and signal times; a Left Behind page sorting every machine by whether it is still working, silent or retired; 3D low-poly worlds and 3D machine models; photos loaded live from the NASA Image and Video Library; and a Mission Debrief where kids learn why NASA leaves hardware behind and vote on what should happen to it: protect it as heritage, bring some home to museums, reuse parts, or clean up space junk.

PROGRESSION

Players earn Stardust for waking machines, answering quizzes, reading replies and unlocking 16 badges, and climb five ranks from Space Cadet to Space Legend. The Moon is free; finishing a destination and spending Stardust unlocks Mars (150), Venus (300), Space Telescopes (450) and Deep Space (600). Progress saves on the device without an account, or to the cloud with a free account.

FOR JUDGES

No login is needed. The "For judges" tab on the right edge gives 2,000 Stardust, starts a guided 9-stop tour of the key features, and turns on tester tools on the Badges & Stardust page: unlock all destinations, wake all machines, add 1,000 Stardust, or reset.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Most kids know the famous missions but not what happened afterwards. Ghost Rovers turns real NASA history into something kids want to play, so they learn by doing: how rovers are driven, why signals take time, how machines wear out, and what each mission discovered. It works in any browser, on phones and laptops, with nothing to install and no account required, so it suits classrooms and home learning. The Debrief brings in a real, open question about space heritage and space junk, encouraging kids to weigh trade-offs and form their own opinion. We want kids to see that the machines we send out are part of history, and that what we do with them is a decision for their generation.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

- HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript, with no framework, so it loads fast on school devices.

- three.js for the 3D worlds and machine models, built in code from simple shapes.

- Firebase Authentication and Realtime Database for optional cloud saves, with locked-down database rules.

- Netlify for hosting.

- The NASA Image and Video Library API for live photos.

- Browser APIs: Geolocation and Device Orientation for the sky finder, the Web Speech API for Listen, and Vibration for phone feedback.

- Planet and Moon positions calculated in the browser from standard orbit formulas; deep-space probe positions projected from published positions and known speeds.

- AI-assisted coding helped build the app, and AI helped create the logo. The idea, game design and UI/UX are by Team Earthlings, and all mission facts come from NASA sources (listed on the Data & Methods page).

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Instead of a fact sheet, every machine is a "ghost" with its own voice that the player brings back. The game uses real physics as game mechanics: the message wait is the actual light-travel time, the sky finder points at where the machine really is right now, and the rover puzzle mirrors how real drivers plan around delay. The fading-signal timeline lets kids feel the moment a mission went silent.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Accuracy and honesty: facts come from NASA mission pages, every quiz answer can be found in the text, and anything simulated (replies, training steps, the driving map, 3D models) is clearly labelled.

- Age-appropriate writing for 10–14-year-olds, with short logs and clear choices.

- Accessibility: Listen read-aloud, keyboard navigation, screen-reader labels and reduced-motion support.

- Privacy for young users: the full game works without an account.

- Performance and devices: the 3D views load only on larger screens, and phones get the sky finder and vibration.

- Game balance: completing a destination always tops players up so they can afford the next one.

- Judges' limited time: a judge mode and guided tour show everything in a few minutes.

OUR GITHUB LINK: https://github.com/Swayambhav318/Ghost-Rovers
